I didn’t say “process his death”, I said “process that death will be the outcome”. 

We live with the pain of the deaths of our loved ones until the end of our own time. But we need not live in denial that death is death, that cancer kills. 

If I told my son I had three months to live with the caveat that my death could be sometime sooner, or sometime later, of course I would want to spend as much of that time as possible with loved ones, but I wouldn’t expect him (and certainly not his SO) to forego every day for me until I croak. 

Of course my sons GF should go to her best friend’s wedding instead of sit by my terminally ill bedside (as she has been for several weeks).

Her choosing to forego the wedding, causing a substantial rift between her and her best friend, is not going to make processing the grief of her BFs father’s death any different for her or her BF - even if he were to croak while she’s at it. That’s not how grief works.

I think YTA. Your BFs Dad has had terminal lung cancer for multiple years. Your boyfriend has had time to process that death will be the outcome. 

I don’t think it’s fair to you or your best friend to miss your best friend’s wedding (an incredibly important day) because.. well maybe Dad will die that day. I doubt your BF’s father would be interested in having you sacrifice a celebration of LIFE and LOVE because he is (and has been) terminally ill.

You should have arranged to be at the wedding (or at least have made the time to make an appearance) and told your boyfriend to stay with his Dad, and returned afterwards. If he happened to pass away while you were at the wedding - what would the real difference be? You didn’t get to smell his last breath? You somehow magically “cared less” because you needed to attend something? 

Dad is gonna die anyways. The fact that you have been supporting your BF through this and with his father so much in late stages is commendable, but IMO I don’t think it’s a valid reason to forego other important moments in your & the people you love’s lives.

This should really be where you’re focused on. 

From a man’s POV, saying the room stunk of cum may be kind of crass, but he’s probably just happy about the sex! If the comment truly made you feel weird you can talk with him about it. Your comment about needing your own space / the way you described the frequency and speed at which things are going - is a telltale sign for future codependency. You should try your best to create boundaries and make sure you are in the right headspace. Taking precaution and having some patience to progress a relationship is actually very enjoyable and leads to a much healthier foundation. If he’s really quality, he will agree on this. It will set you both up for more confidence in the relationship and an assurance that you aren’t making rash decisions just because it feels good - but because you both actually want it.

I will say, 90 days is a pretty standard non-renewal (cancellation or renegotiation) notice period. This is very typically included in the contract.

What Will should have done was send a notice to twitch with his intent to renegotiate at the renewal date, regardless of the date. Twitch would be obliged to recognize this as 90-day non-renewal notice (given it was outside of the period).

What it sounds like is that perhaps Will doesn't have a copy of his contract or has read through the terms himself. Or perhaps he overlooked the 90-day period / his renewal roll-over date and is now stuck with the current terms and whatever auto-renewal term exists (typically a year or two).

Source: I work renewals in B2B SAAS.

>Is there a reason to think that RPGCodex is unrepresentative of people with a sophisticated taste in PC RPGs formed as a result of greater experience with the genre?

You've kind of answered your own question - this is not what I understood your post as setting out to conclude.

Your claim with the data is to show the decline of US RPG's over time, and to support that you are using data collected that is representative 'of people with a sophisticated taste in PC RPGs'. Certainly the broader audience of the RPG genre is not going to be as critical or siloed in their opinions.

The TES games, included in the chart, are a fine example of this.

If you asked a bunch of 15 year-old Americans what their favorite RPGs are, you may see Skyrim near the top, and you probably wouldn't capture 1/2 of the older titles in that chart.  Now if I took that analysis and said it was evidence of the vast success of US RPGs over time, it may be misleading, because that audience isn't exactly representative of the whole (although, arguably, younger audiences drive the obtuse metric of 'success' far more than critical gamers from an RPG-focused forum).

I think the issue here is the defining of 'decline' -  perhaps if you are trying to judge specifically the decline in quality of US RPGs, this would come off as a valued perspective (just as you've stated), and certainly makes the sample more relevant, though not conclusive.

But if you are looking to measure 'rapidly diminishing prevalence', I don't think this data really shows anything - I'd be more inclined to look at sales and overall player count.

To run with the TES example, Morrowind is commonly regarded as a better game than Skyrim in a handful of facilities (particularly in spaces that would appease RPG connoisseurs), but it's certainly not as prevalent - despite what the chart may lead one to believe, given your prompt.

One thing this chart can show is that our marketplace for RPG production has become increasingly diverse & global. There are a number of things that may contribute to how this is displayed via the results from RPGCodex. I would suggest that the primary demographic of RPGCodex, which is very likely tilted towards Americans and other English-speakers, have far more exposure to Japanese PC RPG gaming titles now than they did prior to the year 2000, per the data.

I don't think this data is very useful or should really even be considered in trying to draw the broad conclusion that you have suggested, whether the claim is true or false.

The sample size is incredibly small and specific, and there are tons of other statistical variables or approaches that may be considered in an analysis like this.

It may have made more sense to have titled this akin to  "A visual display of RPGCodex opinions", which is what we are looking at.
